<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Agents</span>, language model (LM)-based systems that are capable of reasoning, planning, and acting are becoming the dominant paradigm for real-world AI applications. Despite this widespread adoption, the principles that determine their performance remain underexplored, leaving practitioners to rely on heuristics rather than principled design choices. We address this gap by deriving quantitative <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">scaling principles</span> for agent systems. We define this scaling as the interplay between the number of agents, coordination structure, model capability, and task properties. We evaluate this across four diverse benchmarks: <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Finance-Agent</span>, <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BrowseComp-Plus</span>, <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">PlanCraft</span>, and <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Workbench</span>, spanning financial reasoning, web navigation, game planning, and workflow execution. Using five canonical agent architectures (Single-Agent System and four Multi-Agent Systems: Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid), instantiated across three LLM families, we perform a controlled evaluation spanning 180 configurations, standardizing tools, prompt structures, and token budgets to isolate architectural effects from implementation confounds. We derive a predictive model using empirical coordination metrics, including efficiency, overhead, error amplification, and redundancy, that achieves cross-validated <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}{=}0.513" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.513</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}{=}0.513</annotation></semantics></math>, enabling prediction on unseen task domains by modeling task properties rather than overfitting to a specific dataset. We identify three dominant effects: <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> a <span id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tool-coordination trade-off</span>: under fixed computational budgets, tool-heavy tasks suffer disproportionately from multi-agent overhead. <span id="abstract1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> a <span id="abstract1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">capability saturation</span>: we observe that coordination yields diminishing or negative returns (<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta{=}{-}0.408" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.408</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta{=}{-}0.408</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p{&lt;}0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p{&lt;}0.001</annotation></semantics></math>) once single-agent baselines exceed an empirical threshold of <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}45\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>45</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}45\%</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="abstract1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3)</span> <span id="abstract1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">topology-dependent error amplification</span>: independent agents amplify errors <math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="17.2{\times}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>17.2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17.2{\times}</annotation></semantics></math> through unchecked propagation, while centralized coordination contains this to <math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.4{\times}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.4{\times}</annotation></semantics></math>. Crucially, coordination benefits are task-contingent. Centralized coordination improves performance by <math id="abstract1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>80.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80.9\%</annotation></semantics></math> on parallelizable tasks like financial reasoning, while decentralized coordination excels on dynamic web navigation (<math id="abstract1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+9.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>9.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+9.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="abstract1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>). Yet for sequential reasoning tasks, every multi-agent variant we tested degraded performance by <math id="abstract1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="39" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>39</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="abstract1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="70\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70\%</annotation></semantics></math>. The framework predicts the optimal coordination strategy for 87% of held-out configurations, providing a quantitatively predictive principle of <span id="abstract1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">agentic scaling</span> based on measurable task properties.</p>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2512.08296v1/agent-scaling_main_v4.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/167;" width="476" height="167" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S0.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agent Scaling across model intelligence and system architectures.</span>
Average performance (%) across four agentic benchmarks improves consistently with increasing model <em id="S0.F1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Intelligence Index</em> (see Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Model Intelligence Index ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>) across three major LLM families (OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic) under different agent configurations. Single Agent System (<span id="S0.F1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SAS</span>) serves as reference trajectories, while Multi Agent System (<span id="S0.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MAS</span>) variants (Centralized, Decentralized, Independent, and Hybrid) reveal distinct scaling behaviors (see Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Benchmark Design Principles. ‣ 3.2 Agentic Tasks and Benchmarks ‣ 3 Agent Systems and Tasks ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for architecture comparisons).
All percentage deltas annotated in the figure (e.g., +8.1%, +8.7%, –4.6%) indicate relative performance change of the best-performing MAS variant compared to the SAS baseline at the same Intelligence Index.
Centralized and hybrid coordination generally yield superior scaling efficiency, suggesting that collaborative agentic structures amplify capability gains more effectively than individual scaling alone.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Agents</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, language model-driven systems that operate through iterative cycles of reasoning, planning, and acting, adapting their behavior based on environmental or tool-generated feedback, have achieved remarkable performance in diverse applications, from code generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, web browsing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, medical decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heydari et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">McDuff et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, finance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, to scientific discovery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gottweis et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mitchener et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. As tasks grow in complexity and require sustained environmental interaction, the field has increasingly turned to multi-agent systems (MAS), relying on the premise that specialized collaboration consistently outperforms single-agent systems (SAS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Previous work has made positive claims about multi-agent systems: “<span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">More agents is all you need</span>” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, suggesting that agent collaboration follows <span id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">collaborative scaling principles</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and that MAS consistently outperforms single-agent systems (SAS) on complex tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>. Yet, despite rapid adoption, there remains no principled quantitative framework to predict when adding agents amplifies performance and when it erodes it. This gap leaves practitioners relying on heuristics, hindering both the emergence of a science of agent systems and, critically for real-world deployment, the ability to determine when multi-agent coordination provides genuine value over simpler single-agent alternatives.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To determine when multi-agent coordination provides benefit, we first establish which task categories require agentic capabilities.
A critical prerequisite is distinguishing between <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">agentic</span> and <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">non-agentic</span> evaluation paradigms. Expanding from the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC) introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we characterize <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">agentic tasks</span> as those requiring: (i) sustained multi-step interactions with an external environment, (ii) iterative information gathering under partial observability, and (iii) adaptive strategy refinement based on environmental feedback.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These characteristics differentiate tasks like web browsing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, financial trading <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, software engineering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and interactive planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> from traditional static benchmarks, tasks solvable through single-shot reasoning without environmental feedback, which lack external environments, are fully observed, or require identical solution strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This distinction matters profoundly because, while recent agentic benchmarks have emerged (e.g., SWE-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barres et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, TerminalBench), <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">multi-agent system evaluations</span> have been conducted predominantly on non-agentic tasks, potentially providing misleading guidance about when collaboration provides value. This distinction is practically consequential: while LLMs achieve high accuracy on isolated code generation tasks like HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, real-world deployment requires agentic capabilities—iterative debugging, repository navigation, and adaptive strategy refinement—as exemplified by interactive coding assistants (e.g., Cursor, Copilot Workspace). Multi-agent systems that show monotonic improvement with team size on static benchmarks (reaching 89% on HumanEval with five agents) exhibit fundamentally different scaling behavior when evaluated on tasks requiring sustained environmental interaction, where coordination overhead and error propagation dynamics dominate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Fundamentally, this distinction reflects a trade-off between context integration and diversity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Single-agent systems maximize context integration by maintaining a unified memory stream in which all reasoning steps share full access to prior history, enabling effectively constant-time access to global context. In contrast, multi-agent systems impose intrinsic information fragmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2025</a>)</cite>: while parallel agents enable diverse exploration, they incur an unavoidable <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">coordination tax</span> in which the global context must be compressed into inter-agent messages. This lossy communication increases synchronization overhead and cognitive load <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_citation ltx_ref_self">malone1994coordination</span>)</cite>, fundamentally altering the scaling behavior of collaboration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The underlying dynamics explain this discrepancy: on agentic tasks, coordination overhead scales with interaction depth, agents operate on progressively divergent world states, and errors cascade through execution chains rather than being corrected through voting. Recent work has identified cases where single strong models match or exceed multi-agent systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, yet the evaluation literature provides limited guidance on <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">what factors</span> determine collaborative success, whether semantic diversity predicts team performance, how architectural choices shape coordination costs, or whether agents can detect and correct failures in extended interactions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The problem is further compounded by rapid progress in frontier model capabilities. As base LLMs gain extended context windows, sophisticated tool use, and improved self-reflection, the unique value proposition of multi-agent collaboration becomes unclear. The answer likely depends on task characteristics and architectural choices that remain to be systematically quantified.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Two fundamental challenges hinder progress toward principled multi-agent design. <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">First</span>, existing MAS evaluations compare architectures using different prompts, tools, or computational budgets, conflating architectural effects with implementation choices and precluding clean causal attribution. <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Second</span>, evaluations focus exclusively on final accuracy metrics without examining process dynamics such as coordination overhead, error propagation, and information flow that determine whether collaboration succeeds or fails. We know from human team performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">McGrath, 1964</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lencioni, 2002</a>)</cite> that team effectiveness depends on composition, coordination mechanisms, and member differentiation. Yet we lack comparable empirical understanding of how these principles translate to artificial agents, leaving practitioners without quantitative guidance for architecture selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we present a controlled evaluation establishing the principles for agent coordination. Our experimental design isolates architectural effects by controlling for implementation confounds which maintains identical task prompts, tools, and computational budgets across all configurations, while systematically varying only coordination structure and model capability. We evaluate five canonical architectures: Single Agent System (SAS) and four Multi-Agent variants (Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid) instantiated across three major LLM families (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) spanning diverse capability levels, on four representative agentic benchmarks: (1) web browsing (BrowseComp-Plus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>), (2) financial analysis (Finance-Agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bigeard et al., 2025</a>)</cite>), (3) game planning (PlanCraft <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>), and (4) realistic workplace tasks (Workbench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Styles et al., 2024</a>)</cite>). Across <math id="S1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N{=}180" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N{=}180</annotation></semantics></math> controlled configurations with matched token budgets, we derive a scaling principle across tested domains quantifying how performance emerges from empirically measured coordination properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to prior claims that “<span id="S1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">more agents is all you need</span>”, our evaluation reveals that the effectiveness of multi-agent systems is governed by quantifiable trade-offs between architectural properties and task characteristics. We establish a predictive framework using empirical coordination metrics: efficiency (success/overhead ratio), error amplification factors, message density and redundancy, achieving cross-validated <math id="S1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}{=}0.513" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.513</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}{=}0.513</annotation></semantics></math> (explaining more than half of the performance variance on held-out data) without dataset-specific parameters. Critically, this framework generalizes beyond training configurations:
leave-one-domain-out cross-validation achieves <math id="S1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}{=}0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.89</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}{=}0.89</annotation></semantics></math>, and the model correctly predicts optimal architectures for 87% of held-out task configurations, demonstrating extrapolation to unseen task structures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis identifies three patterns. First, a <span id="S1.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tool-coordination trade-off</span> (<math id="S1.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta{=}{-}0.330" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.330</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta{=}{-}0.330</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p{&lt;}0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p{&lt;}0.001</annotation></semantics></math>): tool-heavy tasks (e.g., 16-tool software engineering) suffer from multi-agent coordination overhead, with efficiency penalties compounding as environmental complexity increases. Second, a <span id="S1.p10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">capability ceiling</span> (<math id="S1.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta{=}{-}0.408" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.408</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta{=}{-}0.408</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.p10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p{&lt;}0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p{&lt;}0.001</annotation></semantics></math>): tasks where single-agent performance already exceeds 45% accuracy experience negative returns from additional agents, as coordination costs exceed diminishing improvement potential. Third, <span id="S1.p10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">architecture-dependent error amplification</span> where independent multi-agent systems amplify errors 17.2-fold versus single-agent baseline through <span id="S1.p10.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unchecked error propagation</span>, where errors made by individual agents propagate to the final output without inter-agent verification, while centralized coordination achieves 4.4-fold containment via <span id="S1.p10.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">validation bottlenecks</span>, where the orchestrator reviews sub-agent outputs before aggregation., catching errors before they propagate to the final response. Performance spans <math id="S1.p10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{+}81\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>81</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{+}81\%</annotation></semantics></math> relative improvement (structured financial reasoning under centralized coordination) to <math id="S1.p10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{-}70\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{-}70\%</annotation></semantics></math> degradation (sequential planning under independent coordination), demonstrating that architecture-task alignment, not number of agents, determines collaborative success. Importantly, optimal architectures vary systematically: decentralized coordination benefits tasks requiring parallel exploration of high-entropy search spaces (dynamic web navigation: <math id="S1.p10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{+}9.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>9.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{+}9.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>), while all multi-agent variants universally degrade performance on tasks requiring sequential constraint satisfaction (planning: <math id="S1.p10.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{-}39\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>39</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{-}39\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.p10.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{-}70\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{-}70\%</annotation></semantics></math>), where coordination overhead fragments reasoning capacity under fixed computational budgets. We synthesize these findings into quantitative architecture selection
rules (Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Scaling principles ‣ 4 Experiments &amp; Results ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) achieving 87% prediction accuracy on held-out configurations. The underlying mechanisms driving these patterns are interpretable: the tool-coordination trade-off arises because multi-agent systems fragment the per-agent token budget, leaving insufficient capacity for complex tool orchestration; the capability
ceiling reflects that coordination overhead becomes a net cost when
baseline performance is already high; and architecture-dependent error amplification stems from the presence or absence of validation bottlenecks that catch errors before propagation. These mechanistic insights enable
practitioners to move from architectural heuristics to principled, measurement-driven deployment decisions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Our primary contributions are:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Controlled evaluation of agent systems:</span> We establish a framework for comparing agent architectures, controlling for implementation confounds to isolate the effects of coordination structure. Our framework spans 180 configurations across three LLM families and four diverse benchmarks, enabling the causal attribution of performance differences to architectural choices rather than stochastic variations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scaling principle for multi-agent systems:</span> We derive a mixed-effects model (<math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}{=}0.513" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.513</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}{=}0.513</annotation></semantics></math>) using empirical coordination metrics, including efficiency (<math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>), error amplification (<math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>), and redundancy (<math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) to quantify how performance emerges from the interplay of reasoning capability and task properties. The analysis identifies dominant inhibitory mechanisms, specifically the <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tool-coordination trade-off</span> (<math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta{=}{-}0.330" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.330</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta{=}{-}0.330</annotation></semantics></math>) and architecture-dependent error cascades, establishing fundamental limits on coordination effectiveness.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Quantitative principles for architecture-task alignment:</span> We demonstrate that agent architecture selection is governed by measurable task features (e.g., decomposability, tool complexity) rather than simple agent scaling. Our framework achieves 87% accuracy in predicting optimal architectures on held-out tasks, enabling principled deployment decisions grounded in predictive models rather than qualitative heuristics.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) versus Single-Agent Systems (SAS)</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Understanding the difference between single-agent and multi-agent systems remains foundational to characterizing architectural effects. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al. (2025)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we define a <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Single-Agent System</span> as one that features a solitary reasoning locus: all perception, planning, and action occur within a single sequential loop controlled by one LLM instance, even when employing tool use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, self-reflection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, or chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Critically, self-reflection mechanisms do not constitute multi-agent collaboration, as they operate within a single decision-making locus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weng, 2023</a>)</cite>. A <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-Agent System</span> comprises multiple LLM-backed agents communicating through structured message passing, shared memory, or orchestrated protocols <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. MAS architectures vary by topology: <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Independent</span> systems aggregate isolated outputs; <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Decentralized</span> enable peer-to-peer exchange <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Centralized</span> route through orchestrators <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite>; <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hybrid</span> combine hierarchical control with lateral communication <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. MAS evaluation has moved beyond early assumptions of uniform superiority <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2025</a>)</cite> towards a nuanced understanding driven by domain complexity. Comprehensive surveys characterize collaboration mechanisms across coordination protocols <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and agent profiling patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. However, there exist empirical challenges: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al. (2025)</a></cite> show benefits diminish as base models improve, with frontier models often outperforming teams; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cemri et al. (2025)</a></cite> identify 14 failure modes (Cohen’s Kappa=0.88); <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2025)</a></cite> achieve comparable performance at 6-45% cost through dynamic architecture search; and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic (2024)</a></cite> report agents consume 15<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> more tokens. Theoretical foundations from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sumers et al. (2023)</a></cite> propose cognitive architectures contextualizing agents within AI’s broader history. The question of <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">when</span> multi-agent coordination provides value over single strong models with tool use remains empirically open, with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al. (2025)</a></cite>’s proposed scaling laws showing no significant universal pattern <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, motivating our systematic evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agentic Tasks and Benchmarks</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">agentic tasks</span> following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2025)</a></cite> as requiring: (1) sustained multi-step environment interactions, (2) iterative information gathering under partial observability, and (3) adaptive strategy refinement from feedback—differentiating tasks like web browsing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, financial trading <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bigeard et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, software engineering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> from static benchmarks. <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Non-agentic tasks</span> evaluate single-shot inference without environmental interaction: GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite> (direct chain-of-thought math), MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite> (parametric knowledge), HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite> (specification-complete coding), and SQuAD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rajpurkar et al., 2016</a>)</cite> (single-pass comprehension). On non-agentic benchmarks, multi-agent systems show monotonic improvement through ensemble effects (89% on HumanEval with five agents), as voting corrects errors without sequential compounding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This distinction matters profoundly: in agentic settings, coordination overhead scales with interaction depth, agents operate on divergent world states (34% overlap after 10 interactions), and errors cascade rather than cancel <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2025)</a></cite> introduce the Agentic Benchmark Checklist addressing flaws causing 100% relative misestimation. Evolution spans <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024)</a></cite>’s 8-environment evaluation (4k-13k responses) to specialized frameworks: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al. (2024)</a></cite> (GitHub resolution), <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2024)</a></cite> (812 web tasks), <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al. (2025)</a></cite> (30% autonomous completion), and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paglieri et al. (2025)</a></cite> (vision-based RL). <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al. (2023)</a></cite> formalizes reasoning-acting synergy; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weng (2023)</a></cite> characterizes agents requiring planning, memory, and tools; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al. (2025)</a></cite> reveals narrow accuracy focus without cost metrics yields needlessly complex agents. Tasks showing MAS advantages in single-shot settings often exhibit opposite patterns under genuine interaction, indicating architectural benefits are task-contingent, motivating our isolation of coordination effects across diverse agentic domains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling Laws and Coordination Mechanisms</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Understanding performance scaling in multi-agent systems requires distinguishing collaborative scaling from neural scaling laws. While neural scaling follows power laws requiring million-fold parameter increases for significant trends <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, collaborative scaling exhibits logistic growth patterns emerging at substantially smaller scales <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024a)</a></cite> explore whether increased LLM calls alone drive performance, finding compound inference systems follow distinct scaling behaviors from single-model training. However, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024a)</a></cite> note collaborative scaling shows no significant universal pattern, suggesting domain-specific rather than general laws. Coordination mechanisms critically determine whether collaboration amplifies or degrades performance: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduce meta-programming workflows mitigating hallucination cascades; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024b)</a></cite> demonstrate emergent behaviors through structured interactions; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2024)</a></cite> provide general multi-agent frameworks. Recent work reveals architecture-task alignment matters more than team size: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2025)</a></cite> achieve superior performance at 6-45% cost through query-dependent configurations; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dang et al. (2025)</a></cite> show puppeteer orchestration improvements stem from compact cyclic structures; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2023)</a></cite> demonstrate peer-to-peer debate effectiveness depends on task decomposability, with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smit et al. (2023)</a></cite> further showing that multi-agent debate does not reliably outperform single-agent strategies such as self-consistency, suggesting benefits are highly task- and hyperparameter-sensitive. These findings collectively indicate coordination benefits arise from matching communication topology to task structure not from scaling the number of agents, establishing the foundation for principled architectural design rather than heuristic “more agents is better” approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Agent Systems and Tasks</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>System Definition</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building on multi-agent system formalism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, an <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">agent system</span> <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}=(A,E,C,\Omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}=(A,E,C,\Omega)</annotation></semantics></math> consists of a set of agents <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math> (where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math>), a shared environment <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>, a communication topology <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, and an orchestration policy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|A|=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|A|=1</annotation></semantics></math>, we refer to this as a Single-Agent System (SAS); when <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|A|&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|A|&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, a Multi-Agent System (MAS). Each agent <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> perceives, reasons, and acts within the shared environment via iterative feedback.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, each agent <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as a tuple <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{i}=(\Phi_{i},\mathcal{A}_{i},M_{i},\pi_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{i}=(\Phi_{i},\mathcal{A}_{i},M_{i},\pi_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, where:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the reasoning policy (typically an LLM)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{i}=\{\text{ToolCall}(t,\theta):t\in\mathcal{T},\theta\in\Theta_{t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>ToolCall</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{i}=\{\text{ToolCall}(t,\theta):t\in\mathcal{T},\theta\in\Theta_{t}\}</annotation></semantics></math> is the action space consisting of tool usage, where <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of available tools (e.g., web search, code execution) and <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> represents valid parameter configurations for tool <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the internal memory</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{i}:\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{i}:\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the decision function mapping observation histories to actions</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The observation history space <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> contains sequences of action-observation pairs. The decision function <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is instantiated by the reasoning policy <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> (the LLM): given a history <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the LLM generates a reasoning trace and selects the next action. For instance, a history <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i,t}=[(\text{``search(query='pandas')''},\text{``Found 5 files''}),...]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>“search(query=’pandas’)”</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>“Found 5 files”</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i,t}=[(\text{``search(query='pandas')''},\text{``Found 5 files''}),...]</annotation></semantics></math> is processed by <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> to produce the next tool call <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{i,t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{i,t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">At timestep <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, agent <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> selects an action <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{i,t}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{i,t}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> according to:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{i,t}=\pi_{i}(h_{i,t}),\quad o_{i,t}=E(\alpha_{i,t}),\quad h_{i,t+1}=f_{i}(h_{i,t},\alpha_{i,t},o_{i,t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{i,t}=\pi_{i}(h_{i,t}),\quad o_{i,t}=E(\alpha_{i,t}),\quad h_{i,t+1}=f_{i}(h_{i,t},\alpha_{i,t},o_{i,t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the environment and <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i,0}=\{s_{0}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i,0}=\{s_{0}\}</annotation></semantics></math> contains the initial task specification. The history update function <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{i}:\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{A}_{i}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{i}:\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{A}_{i}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> appends the new action-observation pair to the agent’s history: <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i,t+1}=f_{i}(h_{i,t},\alpha_{i,t},o_{i,t})=h_{i,t}\oplus(\alpha_{i,t},o_{i,t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⊕</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i,t+1}=f_{i}(h_{i,t},\alpha_{i,t},o_{i,t})=h_{i,t}\oplus(\alpha_{i,t},o_{i,t})</annotation></semantics></math>, subject to context window truncation when <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|h_{i,t+1}|&gt;\text{MAX\_TOKENS}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mtext>MAX_TOKENS</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|h_{i,t+1}|&gt;\text{MAX\_TOKENS}</annotation></semantics></math>. This update mechanism applies uniformly to both SAS and MAS configurations. Communication between agents occurs through explicit message passing in the orchestration layer.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Single-Agent System (SAS).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Single-Agent System</em> contains one reasoning locus (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|A|=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|A|=1</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is the agent set). All perception, reasoning, and action occur within a single sequential loop, producing computational complexity <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(k)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of reasoning iterations. SAS has zero communication overhead and minimal memory <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(k)</annotation></semantics></math>, but limited capacity for decomposition or verification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-Agent System (MAS).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Multi-Agent System</em> is an agent system <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|A|&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|A|&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, where agents interact through communication topology <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> and orchestration policy <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Communication topology <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> defines information flow patterns between agents:</p>
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Independent</span>: <math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math> (no inter-agent communication)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Centralized</span>: <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=\{(a_{\text{orch}},a_{i}):\forall i\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>orch</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\{(a_{\text{orch}},a_{i}):\forall i\}</annotation></semantics></math> (orchestrator-to-agents only)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decentralized</span>: <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C=\{(a_{i},a_{j}):\forall i,j,i\neq j\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\{(a_{i},a_{j}):\forall i,j,i\neq j\}</annotation></semantics></math> (all-to-all topology)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hybrid</span>: <math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=C_{\text{centralized}}\cup C_{\text{peer}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>centralized</mtext></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>peer</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=C_{\text{centralized}}\cup C_{\text{peer}}</annotation></semantics></math> (orchestrator plus limited peer-to-peer)</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The orchestrator <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math> (when present) determines: (i) how sub-agent outputs are aggregated (e.g., majority voting, weighted synthesis), (ii) whether the orchestrator can override sub-agent decisions, (iii) whether memory persists across coordination rounds, and (iv) termination conditions based on consensus or quality thresholds.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">MAS architectures vary by how information and control propagate among agents, creating distinct trade-offs between computation, coordination, and parallelization. Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Benchmark Design Principles. ‣ 3.2 Agentic Tasks and Benchmarks ‣ 3 Agent Systems and Tasks ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> formalizes these trade-offs using asymptotic notations over <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LLM calls</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sequential depth</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">communication overhead</span>, and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">memory complexity</span>. We selected these five architectures to form a <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">structural ablation of coordination mechanisms</span>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Independent</span> isolates the effect of parallelism (ensemble) without communication.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decentralized</span> introduces peer-to-peer information fusion without hierarchy.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Centralized</span> introduces hierarchical verification and bottleneck control.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I3.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I3.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I3.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hybrid</span> examines the synergy of hierarchy plus lateral flexibility.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This design allows us to causally attribute performance gains to specific coordination mechanics rather than generic “multi-agent” effects. Specific configurations include:</p>
<ul id="S3.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I4.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Independent MAS</span>: <math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega=\text{synthesis\_only}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>synthesis_only</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega=\text{synthesis\_only}</annotation></semantics></math>. Each of <math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> agents performs <math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> reasoning iterations independently, then outputs are aggregated (<math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(nk)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(nk)</annotation></semantics></math>). This achieves maximal parallelization but minimal coordination, suitable for ensemble-style reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I4.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Centralized MAS</span>: <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=\{a_{\text{orch}},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>orch</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=\{a_{\text{orch}},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=\{(a_{\text{orch}},a_{i}):\forall i\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>orch</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\{(a_{\text{orch}},a_{i}):\forall i\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega=\text{hierarchical}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>hierarchical</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega=\text{hierarchical}</annotation></semantics></math>. A single orchestrator coordinates <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> rounds across <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> sub-agents (<math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(rnk)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(rnk)</annotation></semantics></math>). Sequential depth equals <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> while parallelization factor remains <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>. This design stabilizes reasoning but creates a bottleneck at the orchestrator.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I4.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I4.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I4.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I4.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decentralized MAS</span>: <math id="S3.I4.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C=\{(a_{i},a_{j}):\forall i,j,i\neq j\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\{(a_{i},a_{j}):\forall i,j,i\neq j\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega=\text{consensus}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>consensus</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega=\text{consensus}</annotation></semantics></math>.
