Agents communicate in <math id="S3.I4.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> sequential debate rounds (<math id="S3.I4.i3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(dnk)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(dnk)</annotation></semantics></math>). Memory complexity is <math id="S3.I4.i3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(dnk)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(dnk)</annotation></semantics></math> as each agent stores its own debate history. This enables consensus formation through peer-to-peer discussion.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I4.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I4.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I4.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I4.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hybrid MAS</span>: <math id="S3.I4.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=\{a_{\text{orch}},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>orch</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=\{a_{\text{orch}},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=\text{star}+\text{peer edges}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>star</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>peer edges</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\text{star}+\text{peer edges}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.I4.i4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega=\text{hierarchical}+\text{lateral}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>hierarchical</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>lateral</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega=\text{hierarchical}+\text{lateral}</annotation></semantics></math>. Combines orchestrated hierarchy with limited peer communication (<math id="S3.I4.i4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(rnk+pn)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(rnk+pn)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.I4.i4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of peer rounds). This inherits orchestrator control while enabling lateral exchange between agents.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Communication vs. Coordination.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We distinguish <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">communication</em> (message passing between agents) from <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">coordination</em> (strategic direction of agent activities). In centralized systems, coordination occurs through the orchestrator’s task decomposition and progress monitoring, while communication involves passing findings between orchestrator and workers. In decentralized systems, communication and coordination are intertwined through debate rounds where agents both exchange information and collectively steer problem-solving direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, SAS represents the minimal unit of agentic computation (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(k)</annotation></semantics></math>), while MAS configurations explore the scaling frontier of coordination complexity—ranging from fully parallel and communication-free (Independent) to fully coupled with peer consensus (Decentralized). These configurations allow us to test whether performance gains arise from <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">agent coordination and specialization</em> or merely from increased compute through ensembling. Our taxonomy covers coordination patterns common in LLM-based agentic systems.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Our taxonomy focuses on <em id="footnote1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">communication topology</em>: one of several orthogonal MAS design dimensions including agent specialization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, memory architecture, and aggregation strategy. Classical coordination mechanisms (e.g., blackboard systems) assume structured message formats rather than natural language, limiting their direct applicability to LLM-based agents. For comprehensive surveys of LLM-based multi-agent systems, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xi et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Agentic Tasks and Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following and extending the framework of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we operationalize a task <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> as <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">agentic</span> when optimal performance <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">substantially</em> benefits from adaptive interaction. Formally, if <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=\{(a_{t},o_{t})\}_{t=0}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=\{(a_{t},o_{t})\}_{t=0}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> represents an interaction trajectory, then:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}[R(\tau)]-\max_{g}\mathbb{E}[R(g(x))]}{\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}[R(\tau)]}&gt;\delta," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}[R(\tau)]-\max_{g}\mathbb{E}[R(g(x))]}{\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}[R(\tau)]}&gt;\delta,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> represents an interactive policy, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> represents any single-forward-pass function, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> measures task success, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math> is a task-dependent threshold, and the expectation is over task instances <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and stochastic environment dynamics. This definition captures tasks where interaction provides meaningful advantage over the best possible single-shot approach.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The expected return of an optimal policy thus hinges on sequential observation–action feedback, requiring agents to gather information, plan, and revise hypotheses under partial observability. Building on the Agentic Benchmark Checklist <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we formalize three necessary properties for agentic benchmarks:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I5" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I5.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I5.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sequential Interdependence</span>: Later actions depend on earlier observations; a one-shot policy cannot achieve high reward.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I5.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I5.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I5.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I5.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Partial Observability</span>: Critical state information is hidden and must be acquired through active querying or tool use.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I5.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I5.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I5.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I5.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adaptive Strategy Formation</span>: The policy must update internal beliefs based on new evidence obtained through interaction.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Benchmarks lacking these conditions (e.g., GSM8K, MMLU) evaluate static reasoning rather than agentic capabilities.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            We note that “agentic” is defined relative to current model capabilities. For instance, GSM8K could be posed as agentic by providing calculator tools, though current LLMs do not <em id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">require</em> such scaffolding. Conversely, tasks that are agentic today (e.g., SWE-Bench) may become solvable via single-shot inference as models improve. Our evaluation focuses on tasks that <em id="footnote2.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">currently</em> require multi-step interaction for non-trivial performance.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why Environment Feedback Matters.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Real-world deployments such as coding assistants, financial analysts, and embodied robots operate under uncertainty and non-stationarity.
Tasks solvable by direct prompting measure linguistic knowledge, whereas agentic benchmarks evaluate the process of intelligence: exploration, adaptation, and coordination.
Hence, our benchmarks are chosen such that (i) base LLMs perform poorly in single-shot mode, and (ii) non-trivial performance requires multi-step environment interaction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmark Design Principles.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extending the framework proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we introduce additional criteria to isolate <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">architectural effects</em>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I6" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I6.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I6.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I6.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I6.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Controlled Tool Interface:</span> identical tool APIs and observation structures for all architectures to eliminate confounds from external feedback quality.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I6.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I6.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I6.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I6.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Controlled for Parametric Knowledge:</span> within each model family, evaluation emphasizes adaptive reasoning over memorized facts. Cross-family comparisons (Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments &amp; Results ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) account for inherent knowledge base differences through baseline normalization.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I6.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I6.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I6.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I6.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action–Observation Loop Length:</span> each benchmark enforces non-trivial trajectory length <math id="S3.I6.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L&gt;3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L&gt;3</annotation></semantics></math> to ensure sequential reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I6.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I6.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I6.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I6.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparative Normalization:</span> scores are normalized to the best single-agent baseline, measuring coordination gain or loss.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">

<tr id="S3.T2.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="S3.T2.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:68.3pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T2.2.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM Calls</span></span>
</span></td>

<p id="S3.T2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.T2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">*</span> <math id="S3.T2.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = max iterations per agent, <math id="S3.T2.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> = number of agents, <math id="S3.T2.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> = orchestrator rounds, <math id="S3.T2.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> = debate rounds, <math id="S3.T2.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> = peer communication rounds, <math id="S3.T2.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> = average peer requests
per round. Communication overhead counts inter-agent message exchanges. Independent offers maximal parallelization with minimal coordination. Decentralized uses sequential debate
rounds. Hybrid combines orchestrator control with directed peer communication.</p></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments &amp; Results</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To establish quantitative scaling principles for agentic systems, we investigate three research questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ1.</span> What factors determine agent system’s performance (e.g., model capability, coordination architecture, task properties, their interactions)? We systematically vary each factor across 180 configurations to quantify their individual and joint contributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ2.</span> Under what conditions does inter-agent coordination improve or degrade agent system’s performance? We examine how task structure (e.g., decomposability, tool complexity, sequential dependencies) moderates the effectiveness of different architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ3.</span> Can we derive quantitative scaling principles that predict best agent architecture for a given task from measurable properties? We fit a mixed-effects model using empirical coordination metrics to test whether continuous properties outperform categorical architecture labels in explaining performance variance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2512.08296v1/boxplots_v2.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/353;" width="476" height="353"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
<span id="S4.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparative performance of single-agent (SAS) and multi-agent systems (MAS) across four
diverse benchmarks reveals highly task-dependent scaling dynamics.</span> Box plots show distribution of success rates (scale: 0 to 1, where 1 represents 100% success). Percentage annotations represent <span id="S4.F2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">relative</span> improvement/degradation compared to SAS baseline: <math id="S4.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\text{mean}_{\text{MAS}}-\text{mean}_{\text{SAS}})/\text{mean}_{\text{SAS}}\times 100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>mean</mtext><mtext>MAS</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mtext>mean</mtext><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mtext>mean</mtext><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\text{mean}_{\text{MAS}}-\text{mean}_{\text{SAS}})/\text{mean}_{\text{SAS}}\times 100\%</annotation></semantics></math>. SAS serves as the reference baseline (shown without percentage annotation).
<span id="S4.F2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> BrowseComp-Plus shows polarized results, with independent agents catastrophically
underperforming relative to SAS (-35%) while more structured coordination achieves modest gains.
<span id="S4.F2.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> Finance Agent demonstrates the strongest multi-agent benefits, with all MAS architectures
substantially outperforming SAS (from +57 to 81%), suggesting that complex planning and
distributed reasoning provide significant advantages in structured economic domains.
<span id="S4.F2.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span> PlanCraft exhibits consistent degradation across all MAS variants (from -70% to -39%). The core difference from Finance Agent lies in task structure, where Finance Agent tasks decompose into parallelizable subtasks (e.g., separate agents can independently analyze revenue trends, cost structures, and market comparisons, then synthesize findings), whereas PlanCraft requires strictly sequential state-dependent reasoning, each crafting action modifies the inventory state that subsequent actions depend upon. <span id="S4.F2.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d)</span> Workbench shows marginal effects (from -11 to +6%), suggesting balanced trade-offs
between problem structure and orchestration costs.
White diamond markers denote per-architecture mean performance.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted 180 experiments across four representative benchmarks spanning deterministic to open-world task structures: <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Workbench</span> (deterministic code execution and tool use with objective pass/fail criteria), <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Finance Agent</span> (multi-step quantitative reasoning and risk assessment), <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PlanCraft</span> (spatiotemporal planning under constraints), and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BrowseComp-Plus</span> (dynamic web navigation, information extraction, and cross-page synthesis). BrowseComp-Plus exhibits the highest performance variability across experimental configurations (coefficient of variation <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma/\mu=0.32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma/\mu=0.32</annotation></semantics></math> computed across all 45 BrowseComp-Plus runs spanning architectures and model families, where <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is the standard deviation of success rates and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean success rate). By comparison, Workbench (CV=0.12), Finance Agent (CV=0.18), and PlanCraft (CV=0.21) show lower variability, indicating more stable performance across configurations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLMs and intelligence Scaling.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate three LLM families across multiple model sizes, spanning externally standardized Intelligence Index values from 34 to 66 (a composite capability score integrating reasoning, coding, and knowledge benchmarks; see Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Model Intelligence Index ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>):</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.5em;">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenAI:</span> <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">GPT-5-nano, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Google:</span> <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Gemini 2.0 Flash, 2.5 Flash, 2.5 Pro</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Anthropic:</span> <span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Claude Sonnet 3.7, 4.0, 4.5</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Strong consistency across families validates that coordination scaling follows model-agnostic principles: the maximum difference in architecture-specific scaling slopes between any two LLM families is <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\max}=0.023" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.023</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\max}=0.023</annotation></semantics></math> (computed as <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{i,j}|\hat{\beta}_{\text{arch},i}-\hat{\beta}_{\text{arch},j}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mtext>arch</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mtext>arch</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{i,j}|\hat{\beta}_{\text{arch},i}-\hat{\beta}_{\text{arch},j}|</annotation></semantics></math> across families <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i,j\in\{\text{OpenAI, Google, Anthropic}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>OpenAI, Google, Anthropic</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i,j\in\{\text{OpenAI, Google, Anthropic}\}</annotation></semantics></math>), with coefficient of variation CV <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.02</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.02</annotation></semantics></math> across families. To ensure computational fairness, we matched maximum total iterations between MAS and SAS systems: MAS configurations received equal computational budget through parallel agent processing (smaller per-agent iterations for <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-agent teams), while SAS received proportionally more reasoning rounds to compensate for lack of parallel deliberation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agent Architectures and Complexity.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We tested five coordination topologies: Single-Agent System (SAS) and Multi-Agent System (MAS) topologies: Independent (no inter-agent communication), Centralized (hub-and-spoke with orchestrator), Decentralized (peer-to-peer mesh), and Hybrid (dense but curated selective connections). Coordination complexity is parameterized as <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=E/E_{max}\cdot\log n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=E/E_{max}\cdot\log n</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of directed communication edges and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> the team size. This formulation reflects that (i) coordination cost scales with the number of communication channels (<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>), and (ii) message routing complexity grows logarithmically with team size under hierarchical or structured topologies, analogous to routing depth in balanced tree structures where path length scales as <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log n)</annotation></semantics></math>, consistent with distributed systems theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Malone and Crowston, 1994</a>)</cite>. For teams of 3–4 agents, this yields <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C\in[0.35,1.8]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.35</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C\in[0.35,1.8]</annotation></semantics></math>: SAS has <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=0</annotation></semantics></math> (no edges), Independent has <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=0.35" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.35</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=0.35</annotation></semantics></math> (synthesis-only aggregation), and Hybrid reaches <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=1.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=1.8</annotation></semantics></math> (dense peer connections plus orchestrator).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics and Validation.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Primary outcome is task success/accuracy (domain-dependent: factual correctness for Finance Agent, task completion for Workbench, goal satisfaction for PlanCraft, page synthesis accuracy for BrowseComp-Plus). Secondary metrics include: (i) factual error rate <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> via domain-specific validators (Cohen’s <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>: Finance Agent <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.91" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.91</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.91</annotation></semantics></math>, Workbench <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.89</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.89</annotation></semantics></math>, PlanCraft <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.87" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.87</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.87</annotation></semantics></math>, BrowseComp-Plus <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=0.88" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>0.88</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=0.88</annotation></semantics></math>; all exceeding the substantial agreement threshold of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.80</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.80</annotation></semantics></math>); (ii) information gain <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> from pre- vs. post-coordination uncertainty proxies (see Eq. <a href="#A4.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ D.5 Information Gain Computation ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>); (iii) token-overlap structure across agent rationales, labeling tokens as unique (appearing in exactly one agent), shared (two or more agents), or contradictory (semantic opposition detected when BERTScore similarity <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.3</annotation></semantics></math> between assertion pairs, i.e., <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\text{BERTScore}&gt;0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext>BERTScore</mtext></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\text{BERTScore}&gt;0.7</annotation></semantics></math>, following the dissimilarity threshold established by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2019)</a></cite>); (iv) efficiency metrics including success per 1,000 tokens and cost-normalized performance. All metrics are normalized per reasoning turn and per token to enable cross-architecture comparison. We select coordination metrics based on two criteria: (i) direct measurability from experimental traces without requiring ground-truth labels beyond task success, and (ii) coverage of distinct aspects of coordination–performance relationships identified in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cemri et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We excluded metrics requiring subjective human annotation (e.g., solution creativity) or those exhibiting high collinearity with included measures (e.g., total message count correlates <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r&gt;0.92" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.92</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r&gt;0.92</annotation></semantics></math> with overhead). Variance inflation factor (VIF) analysis confirmed no severe multicollinearity among retained predictors (all VIF <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;5</annotation></semantics></math>). Specifically:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.5em;">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coordination overhead</span> <math id="S4.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O=(T_{\text{MAS}}-T_{\text{SAS}})/T_{\text{SAS}}\times 100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>MAS</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O=(T_{\text{MAS}}-T_{\text{SAS}})/T_{\text{SAS}}\times 100\%</annotation></semantics></math>: captures computational cost, identified as a primary bottleneck in production multi-agent deployments.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Message density</span> <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> (inter-agent messages per reasoning turn): quantifies communication intensity, a key factor in coordination scaling.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Redundancy rate</span> <math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> (mean cosine similarity of agent output embeddings): measures agent agreement, relevant for ensemble-based error correction.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coordination efficiency</span> <math id="S4.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}=S/(T/T_{\text{SAS}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}=S/(T/T_{\text{SAS}})</annotation></semantics></math> (success normalized by relative turn count): normalizes success by cost for deployment decisions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error amplification</span> <math id="S4.I2.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{e}=E_{\text{MAS}}/E_{\text{SAS}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>MAS</mtext></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{e}=E_{\text{MAS}}/E_{\text{SAS}}</annotation></semantics></math> (relative failure probability): directly tests whether MAS corrects or propagates errors.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">MAS exhibits domain-dependence with architectural variation.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-agent systems demonstrate highly heterogeneous performance across task domains, contingent on problem structure and architectural choices. On Finance Agent, MAS achieve substantial improvements: Centralized reaches <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+80.9%</span> (mean 0.631 vs. SAS 0.349), Decentralized achieves <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+74.5%</span> (0.609), and Hybrid reaches <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+73.2%</span> (0.604), driven by opportunities for distributed financial reasoning across multiple agents. On Workbench, multi-agent systems show minimal gains: Decentralized achieves <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+5.7%</span> (0.664 vs. SAS 0.629), while Centralized and Hybrid both slightly underperform at <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">-1.2%</span>. On BrowseComp-Plus, improvements remain modest: Decentralized achieves <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+9.2%</span> (0.347 vs. SAS 0.318), with Centralized essentially flat at <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+0.2%</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Critically, PlanCraft exhibits universal performance degradation across all multi-agent architectures. Centralized declines to <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">-50.4%</span> (0.282 vs. SAS 0.568), Decentralized to <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">-41.4%</span> (0.332), Hybrid to <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">-39.0%</span> (0.346), and Independent to <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">-70.0%</span> (0.170). This degradation reveals a <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">coordination-saturation effect</span>: beyond a critical reasoning–communication trade-off, additional coordination no longer improves but suppresses effective reasoning, marking the onset of communication overload. Aggregating across all benchmarks and architectures, the overall mean MAS improvement is <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">-3.5%</span> (95% CI: <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[-18.6%, +25.7%]</span>), reflecting substantial performance heterogeneity with high variance (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=45.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>45.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=45.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>). The performance range across MAS variants spans from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-70.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>70.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-70.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> (PlanCraft Independent) to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+80.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>80.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+80.9\%</annotation></semantics></math> (Finance Centralized), indicating that MAS do not provide universal benefits but rather domain-specific trade-offs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Domain Complexity Moderates Coordination Efficacy.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Mixed-effects regression confirms domain complexity (refer to Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Domain Complexity ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for more details) as a significant negative moderator of MAS advantage (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}=-0.114" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.114</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}=-0.114</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> CI: <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-0.186,-0.042]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.186</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.042</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-0.186,-0.042]</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.002" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.002</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.002</annotation></semantics></math>). The mechanism operates through fixed computational budgets (matched total tokens across MAS and SAS): in structured, decomposable domains (Finance Agent, moderate Workbench instances), agents complete local reasoning with residual capacity available for inter-agent communication. Here, inter-agent messages reduce variance through redundancy elimination and enable synthesis of partial solutions, producing large performance deltas (Finance: <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+80.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>80.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+80.9\%</annotation></semantics></math>). Conversely, in high-complexity sequential domains (PlanCraft), intra-agent reasoning for constraint verification and state tracking consumes most available tokens before communication can occur; subsequent inter-agent messages then compress reasoning quality and produce strong negative returns (PlanCraft: <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-39.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>39.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-39.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-70.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>70.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-70.0\%</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This trade-off is directly quantified by benchmark complexity, operationalized as the average number of sequential reasoning steps required for task completion (normalized to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>). We define a <em id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reasoning step</em> as a single environment interaction. Tool call, state query, or action execution and count steps as the median number of interactions required by the best-performing SAS configuration to reach task completion across all instances in each benchmark: Workbench (0.000, minimal sequential constraints) and Finance Agent (0.407, moderate decomposability) show positive MAS returns or minimal overhead, while PlanCraft (0.419, high sequential dependencies) and BrowseComp-Plus (0.839, dynamic state evolution) show degradation or minimal gains. Domain complexity alone does not fully predict MAS effectiveness. While low-complexity domains (Workbench, D = 0.00) show modest gains and high-complexity domains (BrowseComp-Plus, D = 0.84) show limited benefits, the critical factor is task decomposability: Finance Agent (D = 0.41) achieves +80.9% gains through parallelizable subtask structure, whereas PlanCraft (D = 0.42) degrades by -70% due to strict sequential dependencies despite similar complexity scores. This suggests that sequential interdependence, rather than complexity alone, determines coordination viability. Information gain <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> correlates with this pattern: Finance Agent (structured domain) exhibits strong information-value convergence (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.71" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.71</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.71</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>), while PlanCraft (sequential constraints) shows weak correlation (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.18" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.18</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.18</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.22" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.22</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.22</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating that agents in high-complexity domains exchange limited actionable information due to inherent sequential dependencies and state-space ambiguity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architecture-LLM Family Interactions Reveal Vendor-Specific Coordination Mechanisms.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While domain complexity broadly moderates MAS effectiveness, the architecture-domain interaction reveals <em id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">non-uniform</em> preferences even within similar complexity regimes: no single architecture dominates across all domains and vendors. Architecture effectiveness depends critically on domain structure: <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Finance Agent</span> benefits most from Centralized (+80.9%) and Decentralized (+74.5%), <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Workbench</span> from MAS-Decentralized (+5.7%), and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BrowseComp-Plus</span> from MAS-Decentralized (+9.2%). In degrading domains, architecture selection becomes a least-worst optimization: <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">PlanCraft</span> shows Hybrid as relatively best (-39.0%) compared to MAS-Centralized (-50.4%) and MAS-Independent (-70.0%).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Family-specific coordination preferences emerge within improvement-positive domains. On <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Finance Agent</span>, Anthropic’s MAS-Centralized achieves +127.5% (0.636 vs. 0.280 SAS), indicating conservative but stable coordination, whereas Google’s MAS-Centralized reaches +164.3% (0.740 vs. 0.280 SAS, averaging Centralized performance), suggesting stronger attention-mechanism alignment with hierarchical message exchange; OpenAI’s MAS-Centralized achieves +71.2% (0.79 vs. 0.465 SAS). On <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Workbench</span>, where multi-agent overhead is less tolerable (efficiency degrades from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}=0.466" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.466</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}=0.466</annotation></semantics></math> for SAS to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}=0.074" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.074</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}=0.074</annotation></semantics></math> for Hybrid, the largest relative drop across benchmarks), Anthropic’s best variant (MAS-Decentralized, +10.8%) remains superior to Google (+9.5%) and OpenAI (+8.6%), reflecting relative efficiency in managing coordination costs. Critically, on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">PlanCraft</span> where all variants degrade, vendor preferences flatten: Anthropic shows maximum -54.5% (MAS-Hybrid 0.31 vs. SAS 0.68), Google shows -25.3% (best), and OpenAI shows -32.3%, indicating that communication mechanisms cannot overcome fundamental sequential reasoning constraints. While the precise mechanisms remain to be characterized, potential factors include differences in instruction-following fidelity, context utilization patterns, and inter-turn consistency that affect how agents interpret and respond to coordination messages. No vendor achieves universal multi-agent dominance; instead, each exhibits relative advantages in structured domains (Finance) that evaporate in sequential constraint-satisfaction domains (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">PlanCraft</span>), indicating that multi-agent benefits are genuinely contingent on problem structure rather than generalizable across task types.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2512.08296v1/cost_performance.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/176;" width="476" height="176" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>
<span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cost–Performance Trade-offs Across Model Families and Architectures.</span>
Comparative analysis of single-agent (SAS) and multi-agent (MAS) architectures: Independent, Decentralized, Centralized, and Hybrid across three LLM families.
Each point represents the mean agentic performance (%) versus normalized cost per experiment (USD), with horizontal and vertical error bars denoting Standard Error of Mean (SEM) in cost and performance, respectively.
Notably, the optimal coordination pattern differs across model families: OpenAI models show consistent gains from Centralized and Hybrid MAS configurations despite higher costs, suggesting stronger communication synergy;
Google models display marginal MAS improvements but a clear efficiency plateau, indicating diminishing returns under lightweight coordination;
and Anthropic models reveal higher variance and occasional MAS underperformance, reflecting sensitivity to coordination overhead.
These cross-family discrepancies imply that <em id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">the efficacy of multi-agent coordination is contingent on each model family’s intrinsic communication bandwidth and reasoning alignment</em>.
Collectively, the results uncover a family-dependent scaling law linking coordination structure, economic efficiency, and emergent performance.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Scaling principles</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The main results reveal substantial heterogeneity where agentic system performance ranges from <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+81\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>81</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+81\%</annotation></semantics></math> improvement to <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-70\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-70\%</annotation></semantics></math> degradation depending on task structure and coordination architecture. This variance correlates with measurable properties such as task decomposability, tool complexity, and baseline difficulty. We explore a quantitative principle that not only explains this heterogeneity but also enables <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">prediction</span> for unseen configurations: given measurable properties of a model, task, and system configuration, can we predict a specific agent system’s performance?</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Mixed-Effects Model Achieves 51.3% Cross-Validated Variance Explanation.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We fit a scaling principle to all 180 configurations that relates agentic system performance to four categories of predictors: 1) base model capability (intelligence index <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>), 2) system configuration (agent count <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{a}</annotation></semantics></math>), 3) task properties (tool count <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, single-agent baseline <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{SA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>SA</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{SA}}</annotation></semantics></math>). These are instance-level predictors capturing within-benchmark variation, distinct from the benchmark-level domain complexity <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> defined in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Domain Complexity ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>, and 4) empirically measured coordination metrics from Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ The Scaling Principle Enables Quantitative Architecture Selection. ‣ 4.3 Scaling principles ‣ 4 Experiments &amp; Results ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (efficiency <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, overhead <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O\%</annotation></semantics></math>, error amplification <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, message density <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, redundancy <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>). Rather than including all possible terms, we construct the model based on specific mechanistic hypotheses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Main effects</span> capture direct relationships between individual factors and performance. We include a quadratic term (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) to test for non-linear capability scaling, and log-transformed tool count and agent count following standard diminishing-returns assumptions in scaling analyses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Interaction terms</span> test specific hypotheses about how these factors combine. We include nine interactions, each motivated by observed patterns: <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}\times T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}\times T</annotation></semantics></math> tests whether efficiency penalties compound with tool complexity; <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{e}\times T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{e}\times T</annotation></semantics></math> tests whether errors propagate more severely in tool-rich environments; <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{SA}}\times\log(1+n_{a})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>SA</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{SA}}\times\log(1+n_{a})</annotation></semantics></math> captures the baseline paradox where high single-agent performance leaves less room for coordination gains; <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O\%\times T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo rspace="0.055em">%</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O\%\times T</annotation></semantics></math> tests whether overhead costs scale with task complexity. We deliberately exclude interactions without clear mechanistic justification (e.g., <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R\times c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R\times c</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I\times O\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I\times O\%</annotation></semantics></math>) to avoid overfitting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
