</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Coordination Efficiency, Error Dynamics, and Information Transfer</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy (MAST) proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cemri et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we categorize observed errors into specification, inter-agent misalignment, and verification failures. Building on this taxonomy, we quantitatively analyze error frequency and propagation across architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We systematically characterized coordination efficiency, error propagation mechanisms, and information transfer across all 180 experiments. All MAS and SAS configurations were matched for total reasoning-token budget (mean 4,800 tokens per trial) and tool-call access to isolate coordination effects.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Turn count follows power-law scaling with number of agents.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Total reasoning turns (reasoning–response exchanges) exhibit power-law growth with agent count:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=2.72\times(n+0.5)^{1.724},\quad R^{2}=0.974,\quad 95\%\text{ CI on exponent}:[1.685,1.763],\quad p&lt;0.001." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2.72</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>1.724</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.974</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> CI on exponent</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>1.685</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.763</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=2.72\times(n+0.5)^{1.724},\quad R^{2}=0.974,\quad 95\%\text{ CI on exponent}:[1.685,1.763],\quad p&lt;0.001.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This relationship is fit across architecture-aggregated means; within-architecture variance remains substantial (e.g., at n = 3: Independent averages 11.4 turns vs. Decentralized 26.1 turns), reflecting topology-dependent communication patterns. This super-linear exponent (1.724 <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>) reflects quadratic message complexity (all-to-all potential communication) tempered by practical bandwidth limits, creating a distinct agentic scaling regime fundamentally different from neural network parameter scaling (e.g., Kaplan et al. report <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=0.76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.76</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b=0.76</annotation></semantics></math> for dense models). Empirically, Hybrid systems require 6.2<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> more turns than SAS (44.3 vs. 7.2 turns; <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t(178)=16.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>178</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>16.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t(178)=16.8</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>), while Centralized requires 3.8<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (27.7 turns), and Decentralized requires 3.6<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (26.1 turns). The implication is stark: under fixed computational budgets, per-agent reasoning capacity becomes prohibitively thin beyond 3–4 agents, creating a hard resource ceiling where communication cost dominates reasoning capability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Message Density Exhibits Logarithmic Saturation with Performance.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Success rate follows a logarithmic relationship with message density across all architectures:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=0.73+0.28\ln(c),\quad R^{2}=0.68,\quad p&lt;0.001," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>0.73</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.28</mn><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.68</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=0.73+0.28\ln(c),\quad R^{2}=0.68,\quad p&lt;0.001,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is messages per reasoning turn. Performance plateaus near <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{*}=0.39" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.39</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{*}=0.39</annotation></semantics></math> messages/turn (achieved by Decentralized and Centralized architectures at 0.41 and 0.39 respectively), corresponding to the success rates of 47.7% and 46.3%. Beyond this point, additional messages yield diminishing returns: Hybrid systems (515% coordination overhead, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=44.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>44.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=44.3</annotation></semantics></math>) achieve only <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 2\%</annotation></semantics></math>–3% success gain versus Centralized (285% overhead, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=27.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>27.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=27.7</annotation></semantics></math>), a difference of 0.7 percentage points that is not statistically significant (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t(178)=0.61" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>178</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.61</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t(178)=0.61</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.542" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.542</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.542</annotation></semantics></math>). This saturation reflects fundamental information limits in open-ended reasoning rather than mechanism failures: high-performing runs show convergent token overlap (shared tokens: mean <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 1.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>1.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 1.8</annotation></semantics></math> bits; <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math> vs. low performers) suggesting message consensus is reached; further messages add redundancy rather than novel information.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Error absorption mechanisms.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize error absorption as <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Absorb}=(E_{\text{SAS}}-E_{\text{MAS}})/E_{\text{SAS}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Absorb</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>MAS</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>SAS</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Absorb}=(E_{\text{SAS}}-E_{\text{MAS}})/E_{\text{SAS}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> is factual error rate. The absorption mechanism operates through <em id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">iterative verification</em>: in Centralized and Hybrid architectures, sub-agent outputs pass through an orchestrator that cross-checks reasoning steps before aggregation, enabling detection and correction of logical inconsistencies. In Decentralized architectures, peer debate rounds provide similar verification through explicit challenge-response exchanges. These architectures achieve 22.7% average error reduction (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> CI: <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[20.1\%,25.3\%]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>20.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>25.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[20.1\%,25.3\%]</annotation></semantics></math>), peaking at 31.4% for Finance Agent where structured numerical outputs facilitate verification. Independent MAS shows no error correction (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+4.6\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>4.6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+4.6\%</annotation></semantics></math> amplification) due to absence of any inter-agent verification mechanism where errors made by individual agents propagate directly to the aggregated output without opportunity for correction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The correction mechanism is revealed through token-overlap analysis. Each token in agent rationales is labeled as: (i) unique (appears in exactly one agent); (ii) shared (two or more agents); (iii) contradictory (semantic opposition, BERTScore <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.3</annotation></semantics></math>). High-performing runs exhibit: (i) increased shared-token entropy (mean <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 1.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>1.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 1.8</annotation></semantics></math> bits for Finance Agent; <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math> vs. low-performing runs); (ii) dramatically reduced contradictory mass (median 2.3% in successes vs. 8.1% in failures), evidence that messages converge toward mutually consistent sub-proofs rather than self-reinforcing errors. Interestingly, high redundancy (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R&gt;0.50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R&gt;0.50</annotation></semantics></math>) correlates negatively with success (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=-0.136" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.136</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=-0.136</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.004" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.004</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.004</annotation></semantics></math>), implying an emergent diversity-efficiency trade-off: collective capability peaks when message overlap balances shared grounding with informational diversity; optimal redundancy occurs at <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R\approx 0.41" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.41</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R\approx 0.41</annotation></semantics></math> (Centralized median), balancing information fusion with reasoning independence.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2512.08296v1/heterogeneous.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/186;" width="476" height="186"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agent Heterogeneity Effects on Multi-Agent Performance.</span>
Performance comparison of centralized (Orchestrator-Subagents) and decentralized (Peer Debate with Voting) multi-agent architectures on BrowseComp-Plus benchmark across three LLM families. High-capability models include GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini-2.5 Pro; low-capability models include GPT-5 nano, Claude Sonnet 3.7, and Gemini-2.0 Flash.
(1) Anthropic models uniquely benefit from heterogeneous mixing in centralized architecture, where low-capability orchestrator with high-capability subagents (0.42) outperforms homogeneous high-capability (0.32) by 31%, while OpenAI and Gemini show performance degradation under heterogeneous centralized configurations.
(2) Decentralized mixed-capability approaches achieve near-optimal or superior performance compared to homogeneous high-capability baselines (OpenAI: 0.53 vs 0.50; Anthropic: 0.47 vs 0.37; Gemini: 0.42 vs 0.43), suggesting effective emergent collaboration despite capability asymmetry.
(3) Centralized architectures with low-capability orchestrators underperform dramatically for OpenAI and Gemini families, indicating architectural constraints when coordination relies on less capable models.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Error Taxonomy Reveals Architecture-specific Failure Modes.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We identified four error categories as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">(1) <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Logical Contradiction</span>: agent asserts both “X is true” and “X is false” about the same entity, or derives conclusions violating its stated premises;
(2) <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Numerical Drift</span>: accumulated computational error from cascading rounding or unit conversion mistakes, measured as relative deviation from ground truth exceeding 5%;
(3) <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Context Omission</span>: failure to reference previously established entities, relationships, or state information required for the current reasoning step;
(4) <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Coordination Failure</span> (MAS-specific): message misinterpretation, task allocation conflicts, or state synchronization errors between agents. Architecture-specific patterns emerge across these categories:</p>
<ul id="S4.I3" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.2em;">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Logical Contradiction</span>: Baseline 12.3–18.7%. Centralized reduces to 9.1% (36.4% reduction) via consensus; Decentralized achieves 11.5% through peer verification; Independent unchanged at 16.8%.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Numerical Drift</span>: Baseline 20.9–24.1%. Centralized/Decentralized reduce to 18.3% (24% reduction) via sub-problem verification; Hybrid amplifies to 26.4% as rounding errors propagate; Independent unchanged at 23.2%.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Context Omission</span>: Baseline 15.8–25.2%. Centralized reduces to 8.3% (66.8% reduction) via orchestrator synthesis; Decentralized achieves 11.2%; Independent unchanged at 24.1%.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coordination Failure</span>: Only appears in MAS. Independent: 0% (no coordination mechanism); Centralized: 1.8%; Decentralized: 3.2%; Hybrid: 12.4% (protocol complexity exceeds robust implementation).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These patterns identify three operational coordination regimes: (i) <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Under-coordination</span> (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O&lt;100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O&lt;100\%</annotation></semantics></math> overhead): minimal accuracy gain (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta S\approx+2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta S\approx+2</annotation></semantics></math>–4%), coordination mechanisms not yet engaged; (ii) <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimal band</span> (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200\%&lt;O&lt;300\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mn>300</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200\%&lt;O&lt;300\%</annotation></semantics></math> overhead): highest success–cost ratio (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}\approx 0.16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}\approx 0.16</annotation></semantics></math>), dominated by Centralized and Decentralized, with strong error absorption; (iii) <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Over-coordination</span> (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O&gt;400\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mn>400</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O&gt;400\%</annotation></semantics></math> overhead): Hybrid runs with reduced efficiency (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{c}\approx 0.11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.11</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{c}\approx 0.11</annotation></semantics></math>), protocol complexity introducing coordination-failure modes. Error amplification analysis confirms: Independent architectures propagate errors to 17.2<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> baseline (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math> CI: <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[14.3,20.1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>14.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20.1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[14.3,20.1]</annotation></semantics></math>; no correction mechanisms), while Centralized contains to 4.4<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[3.8,5.0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>3.8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[3.8,5.0]</annotation></semantics></math>) through supervised aggregation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2512.08296v1/architecture_comparison_combined.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/160;" width="381" height="160"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Number of agents scaling reveals model-dependent coordination limits.</span> Performance of Gemini-2.0 Flash (<span id="S4.F5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">a</span>) and Gemini-2.5 Pro (<span id="S4.F5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">b</span>) across multi-agent architectures with varying number of agents (<math id="S4.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{a}\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{a}\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}</annotation></semantics></math>). Both models show initial
gains from multi-agent coordination, but scaling patterns diverge notably:
Gemini-2.0 Flash exhibits a clear optimum at 7 agents before degradation, while Gemini-2.5 Pro’s decentralized architecture peaks earlier despite its higher single-agent baseline. The centralized architecture demonstrates more stable scaling for Flash but shows diminishing returns for Pro beyond 5 agents. Dashed lines indicate single-agent baseline performance. Results suggest that the optimal number of agents depends on both model capacity and coordination strategy, with coordination overhead eventually outweighing parallelization
benefits.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Information Gain (IG) Predicts MAS benefit in Low-Complexity Domains.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compute information gain <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> by comparing pre-coordination and post-coordination task-uncertainty surrogates (via Bayesian posterior variance reduction on key variables). In structured domains (Finance Agent, Workbench), <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> correlates strongly with MAS–SAS gap (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.71" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.71</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.71</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating that agents successfully exchange high-value information and synthesize it into improved solutions. In Finance Agent specifically, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> ranges 0.8–2.1 bits (mean 1.4) for successful trials vs. 0.2–0.6 bits (mean 0.4) for failures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Conversely, in open-world domains (BrowseComp-Plus), <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> shows weak and non-significant power, revealing that agents’ messages provide limited validated information due to inherent world ambiguity. This domain-dependent information-gain pattern directly maps to observed MAS benefits: Finance Agent (+23.1%) where information exchange is high-value; BrowseComp-Plus (+6%–8%) where world ambiguity limits verification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cross-Domain Generalization Validates Coordination Principles.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Architectural rankings remained stable across domains (Kendall <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.89</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.89</annotation></semantics></math>, coefficient of variation <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.1</annotation></semantics></math> across architectures), indicating coordination principles transcend specific task structures. Leave-one-domain-out cross-validation achieved <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.89</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.89</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>), confirming that coordination effects generalize beyond the four benchmarks. Extrapolation to larger teams (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=6</annotation></semantics></math>–10) via the fitted power law yields 95% prediction intervals <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="[3.2,6.8]\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>3.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6.8</mn><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[3.2,6.8]\times</annotation></semantics></math> turn-count increases (bootstrap coverage 94.2%), with high confidence in scaling behavior. Specifically, at <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=6</annotation></semantics></math> agents, predicted turns range from 12.8 to 20.1 (SAS: 7.2; Centralized would reach <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>85</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 85</annotation></semantics></math>–130 turns). This super-linear scaling confirms the hard resource ceiling: beyond 3–4 agents, per-agent reasoning quality degrades sharply under fixed budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Economic Efficiency and Family-Specific Cost-Benefit Trade-offs.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Token efficiency (success per 1,000 tokens) reveals sharp trade-offs by architecture and family: SAS achieves 67.7 successes/1K tokens; Centralized drops to 21.5 (3.1<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> worse); Decentralized to 23.9 (2.8<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> worse); Hybrid to 13.6 (5.0<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> worse). Absolute dollar costs per trial vary by model: OpenAI Hybrid achieves marginal cost <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx\$0.008" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo rspace="0.1389em">≈</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">$</mo><mn>0.008</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx\$0.008</annotation></semantics></math> per 1% success gain (steep but manageable for structured tasks), while Anthropic Hybrid reaches <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx\$0.024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo rspace="0.1389em">≈</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">$</mo><mn>0.024</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx\$0.024</annotation></semantics></math> per 1% gain (3<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> worse, reflecting Anthropic’s sensitivity to coordination overhead). Google maintains intermediate costs <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx\$0.012" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo rspace="0.1389em">≈</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">$</mo><mn>0.012</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx\$0.012</annotation></semantics></math> per 1% gain across architectures, suggesting more balanced cost-benefit trade-offs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM Family-specific Deployment Signatures and Model-Architecture Alignment.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cross-family analysis reveals distinct architectural preferences. OpenAI models show strongest Hybrid synergy on structured tasks (Finance: 52% success Hybrid vs. 39% SAS; Workbench: 56% Hybrid vs. 42% SAS). Anthropic models display most conservative, stable Centralized performance (mean 43% across tasks, SD = 2.3%, lowest variance). Google models exhibit robust cross-architecture efficiency (performance range &lt; 5% across topologies). These patterns (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.89</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.89</annotation></semantics></math> cross-validation) reflect fundamental differences in attention mechanisms, activation sparsity, and representation geometry enabling or constraining multi-agent interaction, not superficial hyperparameter differences.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Limitations and Future Works</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While this work provides quantitative scaling principles for agent systems across architectures and model families, several limitations remain. <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(i)</span> Our framework systematically compares canonical coordination structures (Independent, Decentralized, Centralized, and Hybrid) with preliminary exploration of scaling number of agents up to nine. However, our empirical findings suggest that scaling to larger collectives may face fundamental barriers: the communication overhead we measured grows superlinearly with agent count, and coordination efficiency degrades substantially beyond moderate team sizes. Whether such collectives can exhibit beneficial emergent behaviors, such as spontaneous specialization or hierarchical self-organization, or whether communication bottlenecks dominate remains an open question that parallels phase transitions in complex adaptive systems. <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(ii)</span> While we explore capability heterogeneity by mixing models of different intelligence levels within the same LLM family, all agents share identical base architectures differing only in scale and role prompts. Future work should investigate teams combining fundamentally different model architectures, domain-specialized fine-tuning, or complementary reasoning strategies to understand when <em id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">epistemic diversity</em> yields robustness rather than coordination noise. <span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(iii)</span> Our analysis reveals that tool-heavy environments represent a primary failure mode for multi-agent coordination, with significant negative interactions between tool count and system efficiency. Developing specialized coordination protocols for tool-intensive tasks, such as explicit tool-access scheduling, capability-aware task routing, or hierarchical tool delegation, represents an important direction for improving multi-agent reliability. <span id="S5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(iv)</span> While we controlled prompts to be identical across conditions for experimental validity, we did not optimize prompts specifically for each model or model family. Given known sensitivity of LLM behavior to prompt formulation, architecture-specific prompt tuning may yield different scaling characteristics than those reported here. <span id="S5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(v)</span> Our analysis spans four agentic benchmarks, which, while diverse in task structure (deterministic tool use, quantitative reasoning, sequential planning, dynamic web navigation), may not capture the full spectrum of agentic task characteristics. The strong differentiation in MAS effectiveness across these four benchmarks (Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4 Experiments &amp; Results ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) suggests that additional environments, particularly those with intermediate characteristics or novel task structures such as embodied agents, multi-user interaction, or long-horizon temporal dependencies would strengthen confidence in the identified thresholds and scaling principles. <span id="S5.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(vi)</span> The economic viability of multi-agent scaling remains a practical barrier. As shown in our cost analysis (Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Coordination Efficiency, Error Dynamics, and Information Transfer ‣ 4 Experiments &amp; Results ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>), token consumption and latency grow substantially with agent count, often without proportional performance gains. Future work should explore efficiency-oriented designs, such as sparse communication, early-exit mechanisms, or distilled coordinator models, to make multi-agent deployments economically feasible at scale. Additionally, current agentic benchmarks capture dynamic text-based environments but do not yet include long-horizon temporal dependencies or real-world feedback loops. Integrating embodied or multimodal settings (e.g., robotic control, medical triage, multi-user social interaction) will test whether our observed scaling principles generalize beyond symbolic domains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This study quantifies scaling principles for agentic systems across 180 controlled experiments spanning three LLM families and four agentic benchmarks. We reveal that multi-agent performance exhibits an inverted-U relationship with coordination complexity, with benefits diminishing beyond moderate coordination levels. Domain complexity emerges as the strongest performance predictor (<math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=-0.114" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.114</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=-0.114</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.002" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.002</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.002</annotation></semantics></math>), reducing MAS advantage more substantially than architectural choices. Performance gains vary dramatically by task structure: +80.9% on Finance Agent versus <math id="S6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>70.0% on PlanCraft, indicating that coordination benefits depend tightly on task decomposability. Under fixed computational budgets, turn count grows superlinearly with team size (<math id="S6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\propto n^{1.724}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>1.724</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\propto n^{1.724}</annotation></semantics></math>), constraining effective team sizes to 3–4 agents in practice. We derive a predictive relationship showing that MAS advantage depends on both model capability (<math id="S6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>) and domain complexity (<math id="S6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>), enabling practitioners to estimate expected gains before deployment. Cross-validation achieves <math id="S6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.89</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.89</annotation></semantics></math> on held-out data. Our findings suggest that multi-agent benefits depend critically on task structure rather than team size alone. Effective system design requires matching coordination topology to problem characteristics, rather than assuming uniform benefits from scaling agent count.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<li id="bib.bib38" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_inproceedings"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Du <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">et al.</span> (2023)</span>

<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix" style="font-size:173%;">Appendix</h2>

</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Model Intelligence Index</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify the capabilities of LLMs used in our study, we adopt while extending the <span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">3</span></span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_upright">https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index</a></span></span></span></span>. This index provides one of the most comprehensive publicly available syntheses of model capabilities, combining performance across reasoning, knowledge, mathematics, coding, instruction following, long-context reasoning, and agentic workflow tasks. Its construction integrates ten evaluation suites (e.g., MMLU-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, GPQA Diamond <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, HLE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, AIME 2025, SciCode <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LiveCodeBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, IFBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pyatkin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, AA-LCR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artificial Analysis Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, Terminal-Bench Hard, and <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-Bench Telecom <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barres et al., 2025</a>)</cite>), with careful standardization, robust answer extraction, and model-agnostic prompting.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our study requires a unified, quantitative measure of a model’s baseline capabilities that is <em id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">independent of</em> any agentic mechanism or multi-agent collaboration structure. The Intelligence Index meets this requirement by:
(i) evaluating all models under consistent, zero-shot, instruction-prompted conditions;
(ii) employing pass@1 scoring and robust equality-checker mechanisms;
(iii) reporting a composite measure reflecting general-purpose reasoning and problem-solving ability; and
(iv) demonstrating high statistical reliability (reported confidence interval below <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 1\%</annotation></semantics></math>).
This makes it suitable as a foundational axis for studying <span id="A1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how agentic performance scales with underlying model capacity</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Beyond Artificial Analysis Evaluations.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Artificial Analysis reports Intelligence Index scores for a growing but still limited subset of frontier models. Our work requires a broader coverage, including several models that are not yet benchmarked on the official platform. For these models, we independently reproduced a subset of the Intelligence Index evaluations, specifically AA-LCR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artificial Analysis Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, HLE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, MMLU-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, GPQA Diamond <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, AIME 2025, LiveCodeBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, SciCode <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and IFBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pyatkin et al., 2025</a>)</cite> using the publicly disclosed methodology, prompts, scoring procedures, and evaluation environments described by Artificial Analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the models without publicly available results, we computed a <span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reconstructed Intelligence Index</span> following the equal-weighting formulation used in Intelligence Index v3.0. In cases where full reproduction was infeasible (e.g., specific agentic workflow tasks or unavailable context window limits), we report approximate estimates (denoted with “<math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>”) and discuss their limitations transparently. These reconstructed values should be interpreted as <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">methodologically consistent but not officially certified</em> estimates.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Beyond Artificial Analysis Evaluations. ‣ Appendix A Model Intelligence Index ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> summarizes the reconstructed Intelligence Index and underlying component scores for all models used in our study. The table includes:
(i) official Intelligence Index values when available;
(ii) reconstructed values for non-reported models;
(iii) all constituent evaluation scores used to compute the aggregate index;
(iv) additional model metadata (context window, cost, throughput, latency) relevant for agentic performance analysis.</p>
</div>

<p id="A1.T6.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left ltx_figure_panel"><sup id="A1.T6.3.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="A1.T6.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">∗</span></sup><span id="A1.T6.3.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> Estimated or averaged from reported range.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our reconstructed Intelligence Index values should be interpreted with appropriate caution.
First, several evaluations, particularly long-context and agentic workflow tasks, contain nondeterministic components that may vary slightly across implementations.
Second, for models without public API support for large-context evaluation (e.g., “non-reasoning” checkpoints), our long-context estimates represent upper-bound approximations based on available context windows and internal model behavior.
Third, Artificial Analysis maintains private test variants and additional filtering procedures that cannot be fully reproduced. Thus, our estimates provide a methodologically aligned but not officially verified extension.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Domain Complexity</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We quantify domain complexity through a composite metric that captures empirical difficulty across evaluated benchmarks. This principled approach enables systematic analysis of when multi-agent coordination yields performance benefits versus incurring prohibitive overhead.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Complexity Metric Construction</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Domain complexity <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> is computed as the conservative average of three complementary measures:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance Ceiling.</span> Defined as <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-p_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-p_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> is the highest performance achieved by any evaluated system. Lower ceilings indicate greater inherent task difficulty.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coefficient of Variation.</span> Computed as <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma/\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma/\mu</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> denote the standard deviation and mean of performance across all configurations. This scale-invariant measure captures relative variability independent of absolute performance ranges.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Best-Model Baseline.</span> Defined as <math id="A2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-p_{\text{best}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>best</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-p_{\text{best}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{best}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>best</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{best}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the state-of-the-art single-model performance on each dataset, providing an upper bound on achievable accuracy.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The final complexity score is the arithmetic mean of these three components, yielding a robust estimate that mitigates sensitivity to any single measure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Domain Characterisation</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ B.2 Domain Characterisation ‣ Appendix B Domain Complexity ‣ Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> summarises the complexity scores and defining characteristics of each benchmark.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Domain complexity scores and task characteristics.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Critical Threshold</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis identifies a critical complexity threshold at <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\approx 0.40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\approx 0.40</annotation></semantics></math>. Below this threshold, multi-agent architectures yield net positive returns through effective task decomposition and parallel reasoning. Above this threshold, coordination overhead consumes computational resources otherwise allocated to reasoning, resulting in performance degradation. This finding suggests that the suitability of multi-agent approaches is fundamentally constrained by domain-intrinsic properties rather than architectural sophistication alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Datasets</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our agent systems across four agentic benchmarks requiring multi-step reasoning and tool interaction. Each dataset emphasizes different aspects of agentic behavior: information retrieval, domain expertise, planning, and task decomposition.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Finance Agent.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the Finance Agent benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bigeard et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, comprising 50 finance questions requiring domain expertise and multi-step analysis. Tasks include earnings analysis, financial metric calculations, and market trend interpretation. Each instance includes expert-provided rubrics for structured evaluation. Questions typically require 15-30 minutes of expert time, indicating substantial complexity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">BrowseComp Plus.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BrowseComp Plus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> contains 100 web browsing tasks requiring multi-website information synthesis. Tasks include comparative analysis, fact verification, and
comprehensive research across multiple web sources. Each instance requires agents to navigate complex information landscapes, extract relevant details, and synthesize findings. The dataset uses LLM-based evaluation comparing agent responses against ground truth answers with confidence scoring.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">WorkBench.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">WorkBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Styles et al., 2024</a>)</cite> evaluates business task automation through function calling sequences. The dataset covers five domains: analytics, calendar management, email
operations, project management, and customer relationship management. Success requires executing correct tool sequences to accomplish realistic business workflows. Evaluation follows outcome-centric assessment, measuring exact match between predicted and expected function call sequences. The dataset supports 100 distinct business scenarios with tolerance for minor date variations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Plancraft.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Plancraft <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> focuses on sequential planning in Minecraft environments. Agents must craft target items by determining optimal action sequences using available inventory and crafting recipes. Tasks require multi-step reasoning about dependencies, resource management, and action ordering. The dataset uses environment-determined success
metrics based on successful item crafting within step limits. We use the plancraft-test subset containing focused planning challenges.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Implementation Details</h2>

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Technical Infrastructure</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our implementation leverages LiteLLM<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.litellm.ai/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.litellm.ai/</a></span></span></span> for unified API access across model providers and LangChain<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.langchain.com/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.langchain.com/</a></span></span></span> for agent orchestration and tool integration. LiteLLM provides standardized interfaces for OpenAI, Gemini, and Anthropic models, enabling seamless model switching and comparison. LangChain facilitates tool binding, conversation management, and structured prompting.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">API Integration.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We access LLMs through provider-specific APIs: OpenAI API for GPT models (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5-nano), GenAI API for Gemini models (gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.0-flash), and Anthropic API for Claude models (claude-4.5-sonnet, claude-4.0-sonnet, claude-3.7-sonnet). Our implementation includes intelligent API key rotation across multiple keys per provider to handle rate limiting and quota management. Context window management automatically truncates conversation history when token limits are approached.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tool Environment.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each dataset defines its tool ecosystem through environment configurations. Tools include web search (Tavily<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <a href="https://tavily.com/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://tavily.com/</a></span></span></span>), code execution (Python REPL), mathematical operations, and task
completion markers. Tool definitions use LangChain’s BaseTool interface with structured input schemas and execution methods. Tools are dynamically bound to LLM instances using
function calling capabilities when available.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Agent Configuration</h3>

<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architecture Parameters.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Single agents use maximum 10 iterations per instance. Independent multi-agent systems deploy 3 agents with synthesis-only coordination. Centralized systems employ 3 sub-agents with 1 orchestrator across maximum 5 orchestration rounds, with 3 iterations per agent per round. Decentralized systems run 3 agents through 3 debate rounds with 3 iterations per round. Hybrid systems combine centralized orchestration with limited peer communication phases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Heterogeneous Models.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our framework supports heterogeneous configurations where different agent roles use different models. Orchestrators can use high-capability models (e.g., GPT-5) while sub-agents use
efficient models (e.g., Gemini-2.0 Flash). The LLMConfig class manages model assignment with automatic LLM instance creation for each agent role. Decentralized systems can assign
different models to different workers for diversity.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>Prompt Compilation System</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement a structured prompting system supporting named templates and variable interpolation. Prompts are defined in YAML files with base templates and role-specific extensions.
The compilation process performs template variable replacement using double-brace syntax (variable) and supports conditional template selection based on agent type and conversation state.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dataset Integration.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each dataset provides shared prompt templates containing task-specific instructions and examples. Dataset instances contribute prompt variables including problem descriptions,
context, and constraints. The prompt compilation system merges agent prompts with dataset templates, ensuring consistent instruction delivery across architectures while maintaining task specificity.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>Evaluation Methodology</h3>

<section id="A4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sample Sizes.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on dataset subsets balancing computational cost with statistical significance: Finance Agent (50 instances), BrowseComp Plus (100 instances), WorkBench (100 instances),
and Plancraft (100 instances). Instance selection ensures representative coverage of task types and difficulty levels within each benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Restrictions and Controls.</h4>

<div id="A4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments use identical tool interfaces and observation structures across architectures to eliminate external feedback confounds. Context window management applies consistent truncation policies. API rate limiting and retry mechanisms ensure fair resource allocation. Evaluation uses frozen model weights without fine-tuning to measure architectural effects independently of model optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.5 </span>Information Gain Computation</h3>

<div id="A4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Information gain <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> quantifies the reduction in task uncertainty achieved through agent coordination. We estimate this via Bayesian posterior variance reduction:</p>
<table id="A4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathcal{I}=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\text{Var}[Y|\mathbf{s}_{\text{pre}}]}{\text{Var}[Y|\mathbf{s}_{\text{post}}]}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mtext>post</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathcal{I}=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\text{Var}[Y|\mathbf{s}_{\text{pre}}]}{\text{Var}[Y|\mathbf{s}_{\text{post}}]},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> is the task success indicator, <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{\text{pre}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{\text{pre}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the agent’s state representation before coordination (initial reasoning trace), and <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{\text{post}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mtext>post</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{\text{post}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the state after coordination (final aggregated output). Variances are estimated via Monte Carlo sampling: we generate <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=10</annotation></semantics></math> reasoning traces per state using temperature <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.7</annotation></semantics></math> and compute empirical variance of predicted success probabilities. For binary outcomes, this reduces to:</p>
<table id="A4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Var}[Y|\mathbf{s}]=\hat{p}(\mathbf{s})(1-\hat{p}(\mathbf{s}))," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>𝐬</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐬</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐬</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Var}[Y|\mathbf{s}]=\hat{p}(\mathbf{s})(1-\hat{p}(\mathbf{s})),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS5.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(\mathbf{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐬</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(\mathbf{s})</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean predicted success probability across samples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2512.08296v1/main_exp.png" id="A4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/484;" width="476" height="484" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="A4.F6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmark-specific scaling dynamics across LLM families.</span>
Performance curves across four benchmarks show best-performing multi-agent variants versus single-agent baselines by Intelligence Index. OpenAI and Google exhibit strong cooperative scaling in structured tasks (Finance Agent: <math id="A4.F6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+23.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>23.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+23.1\%</annotation></semantics></math>; Workbench: <math id="A4.F6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+20.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>20.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+20.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>; Cohen’s <math id="A4.F6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d&gt;1.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d&gt;1.2</annotation></semantics></math>). Anthropic models show diminished or negative returns in open-ended environments (PlanCraft: <math id="A4.F6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-35.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>35.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-35.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> for uncoordinated variants; <math id="A4.F6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\approx 0.35" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.35</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\approx 0.35</annotation></semantics></math>), where independent reasoning sometimes outperforms coordination. Cross-family variance decomposition (<math id="A4.F6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0.89</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=0.89</annotation></semantics></math>) confirms that intrinsic communication alignment differences drive these divergent patterns.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"></p>
</div>
</section>
